title: Layered networks: from the cable to the browser

videos.script: Four lessons in, you have met a cable, a packet, an address and a card, and each one arrived on its own. Here is the arrangement that holds them together. {{so-far}} A network is built in layers. Each one does a single job, and talks only to the layer above it and the layer below. {{stack}} That sounds like an organisational chart, and the temptation is to treat it as one — something drawn for a diagram rather than something that runs. It is not. It is the reason the web survived the disappearance of the technology it was invented on. {{claim}} The pages you load today were designed for telephone lines. They now travel over fibre, over radio, over a cable in the sea, and not one line of the page had to be rewritten. {{survived}} That happened because the part that carries and the part that speaks were never allowed to know about each other. Change the bottom, and the top does not notice. {{independence}} By the end of this lesson you will be able to name the layers, say which of the two models is actually running on your machine, and look at a message and tell which layer wrote which part of it. {{title}}

One request, all the way down and all the way back. You have clicked a link, and the browser has a line to send: GET slash index dot html, and the name of the host. {{line}} That is the application layer, and it is the only layer that knows what any of this means. It hands the text down and stops thinking about it. {{hand-down}} Transport takes it. The text is too long for one packet, so it is cut into segments, and each one is numbered. A header goes on the front: this came from port 51000 and is going to port 443. Numbered, so the far side can put them back in order; addressed by port, so the far side knows which program to give them to. {{segment}} Down again, to the internet layer. Now a second header, and this one carries the addresses: from this machine, to that server, somewhere out there. This is the header the routers will read, and the only one they will read. {{ip-header}} Down once more, to the link layer, and a third header — the address of the next card on this wire. Not the server: the router in your house. Two metres, not two continents. {{frame}} And out. {{out}} Watch the first router. It strips the link header, because that one was only good for one hop. It reads the internet header, decides where next, and writes a completely new link header for the next wire. The transport header it never opens. The text it never sees. {{hop}} That repeats at every hop. New envelope each time, same letter inside, and nobody along the way reads the letter. {{repeat}} At the server, the climb. Link header off — this frame was for me. Internet header off — this packet was for me. Transport header off, and the segments are put back in order, because they arrived in the wrong one. {{climb}} And the server's application layer receives exactly the line the browser sent. Byte for byte, after four rewrites and however many hops. {{arrive}} That is what the layers buy. Every one of them can be replaced without telling the others, and the letter comes out the way it went in. {{close}}
